newsitem.title: UK: British shares recoil under threat of rising rates.
newsitem.headline: British shares recoil under threat of rising rates.

text.p: A Bank of England warning of higher inflation risks and rising interest rates dealt British shares a body blow this week, ramming home the shift in prospects following last week's rise in base rates.
"Absolutely there has been a change," said Ian Scott, European equity strategist at broking house Lehman Brothers.

"The rise in interest rates on the back of the strong pound confirmed our view that there is little to go for in the UK market," Scott said on Thursday. "We expect it to come back further between now and end of year."

Despite rising to a record 4,073.2 during October, the FTSE 100 index has underperformed other leading equity markets for much of 1996. And the prospect of rising price pressures during 1997 could lead to further underperformance.
At 1530 GMT on Thursday, the FTSE stood at 3,907.8 points, down 27.9 points, or 0.7 percent from Wednesday's close.
Earlier this week U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch cut its rating on the British equity market to "neutral" from "overweight", worried about Britain's deteriorating economic prospects.

"We are likely to see rate rises and a pick-up in inflation in the UK over the next year," said Merrill strategist Trevor Greetham. "Expected GDP growth of around four percent is a lot stronger than any other major economy."
Yet as strategists look ahead to prospects for British shares during 1997, some argued that the market could perform well as faster economic growth feeds through into higher profits.
"The extent of the pick-up in inflation is not going to be that great, it is hardly rampant inflation," said Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon.
"I can't believe international asset allocators are just going to switch out of the UK where there is going to be a strong economy and a strong currency."

Whether faster growth swings the balance in favour of the British market however remains to be seen and, even if the market rises, better returns may be found in other markets less likely to be troubled by inflation woes -- or in areas such as commodities which actively gain from rising prices.
Merrill's preference is for markets such as Australia, Canada and South Africa where the large number of mining shares is a lure for anyone seeking to invest in commodity plays.

At Lehman Brothers, one of strategists' favoured equity markets is Sweden, with its concentration of "cyclical" shares in basic industries such as paper whose profits are closely linked to swings in the economic cycle.
Behind such recommendations is the battle among strategists and fund managers to switch investments at the right time to pre-empt swings in market sentiment.

At Panmure, Williams expects the FTSE 100 to retreat to 3,800 by year-end before rebounding in 1997. But he points out that domestically-oriented British stocks will be in the front line to gain from faster economic growth.
"We are short-term cautious but if you are looking on a 12-month view you can still argue a reasonably bullish case on fundamental grounds," Williams said.

Rising interest rates however have already propelled sterling higher and with many of Britain's top companies heavily dependent on overseas earnings, a strong pound translates into lower profits once those earnings are brought home.

"We have also been advising people for some time to steer clear of overseas earners, we don't think the market has taken fully on board the impact of sterling's rise," said Scott at Lehman. He expects a modest single-digit return from British equities through the next 12 months.

Meanwhile the jury is still out on the timing and motives of Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's quarter-point rate rise last week. And as the election due by May looms, worries over his handling on the economy are unlikely to go away.
"We felt to try to paint the Chancellor as being prudent at this stage was just a mistake," said Scott. "There was a heavy dose of political judgement in last week's increase."
